findings.title: Password change no longer rotates session_secret, so stolen or old session cookies stay valid for up to 30 days (session hijack persists)
findings.problem: This diff deletes the only thing that logged out other devices when the password changed: generating a new session_secret and saving it with the new password hash. Session cookies are itsdangerous TimestampSigner values that contain only the username (triggarr/auth.py:79-94). They are checked against session_secret alone, with a 30-day max_age (triggarr/auth.py:10, :97-114; middleware triggarr/web/middleware.py:145-148). The password hash is not part of the cookie. So after this change, every cookie issued before a password change keeps working for up to 30 days. That includes a cookie held by an attacker. I found no replacement anywhere: no hash-bound session, no session version, and no server-side revocation list.
findings.fix_hint: Restore the session_secret rotation and the cookie re-issue for the acting user. Mirror reset_confirm_post (routes.py:1941-2005), which still rotates.
findings.why_it_matters: People change their password because they think a session is compromised. This change silently stops that from logging the attacker out. It reverses a documented trust requirement that the tests explicitly check.
source_window: context={"errors": {"new_password": "Password must be 72 characters or fewer"}},

members.title: Stolen session cookies retain access after password changes
members.problem: A stolen, unexpired triggarr_session cookie remains usable after POST /settings/password succeeds because this update preserves session_secret. AuthMiddleware accepts that cookie at triggarr/web/middleware.py:144–148 without checking the password hash; validate_session only checks its signature and 30-day age. An attacker therefore retains authenticated access for the cookie's remaining lifetime despite the owner's password change. The removed secret rotation previously blocked this exact path; rotation in the separate reset endpoint does not protect password changes. Existing test_password_change_invalidates_old_sessions explicitly requires rejection of the old cookie.

members.why_it_matters: A stolen, unexpired triggarr_session cookie remains usable after POST /settings/password succeeds because this update preserves session_secret. The removed secret rotation previously blocked this exact path.
members.fix_hint: Restore session-secret rotation alongside the password-hash update and reissue the acting user's cookie under the new secret. Verify that a second client's pre-change cookie is rejected.

members.title: change_password no longer follows the credential-change pattern that reset_confirm_post mirrors
members.problem: Routes that change credentials share one pattern: write a new session_secret together with the new credential, then sign the acting user's cookie with the new secret. Two other sites in this file follow it: initial setup (routes.py:1294-1341, generate_session_secret, sign_session, set_cookie) and reset_confirm_post (routes.py:1941-2009). The reset_confirm_post docstring (routes.py:1848) calls that route a path 'mirroring change_password' and names the rotation as D-12. This diff takes rotation and cookie re-issue out of change_password only. The two password-change paths now disagree about session invalidation, and the docstring that claims they mirror each other is now false.

members.why_it_matters: Changing your password no longer logs out other devices, but a reset still does. Anyone who changes their password because they think a session is compromised stays exposed. The two routes now drift apart quietly while the code comments say they match.
members.fix_hint: Restore the rotation and cookie re-issue (commit 0866332). If dropping it is intended, record that decision and update the reset_confirm_post docstring and the D-12 rationale to match.

members.title: Password change no longer rotates session_secret, so other sessions stay valid after the change
members.problem: The diff takes out the session_secret rotation in change_password. Session cookies are signed over the username alone (auth.py:79 sign_session(username, secret)). middleware.py:146 checks them with validate_session against auth.session_secret, which this route no longer changes. So every cookie issued before the password change, including one a compromised device holds, stays valid for the full COOKIE_MAX_AGE of 30 days. This drops the session-eviction control that the removed comment described. I found no other check that does the same job: validate_session never looks at password_hash. The reset flow (routes.py:1941) still rotates, which makes the two flows inconsistent.

members.why_it_matters: A user who changes their password because a session may be compromised gets no protection: the attacker's cookie keeps working for up to 30 days.
members.fix_hint: restore generate_session_secret() rotation in the model_copy update and re-issue the acting user's cookie signed with the new secret, as the reset flow does at routes.py:1941-2006

members.title: Password change no longer invalidates existing sessions (revert of documented session-secret rotation)
members.problem: The diff removes the session_secret rotation from change_password (triggarr/web/routes.py). Previously, on password change, new_auth rotated both password_hash and session_secret (model_copy with SecretStr(new_session_secret)), which invalidates every existing session cookie (validate_session checks the signature against the current session_secret) and then re-issues only the acting user's cookie signed with the new secret. The diff now only updates password_hash, leaving session_secret untouched. Any session cookie issued before the password change (the user's own other-device cookies, or a cookie held by an attacker who compromised the account/stole a cookie) remains valid and continues to pass validate_session after the password is changed. The exact same rotation pattern is still present and documented a few hundred lines below in reset_confirm_post (lines ~1937-2009), labeled D-12, confirming this control is still considered load-bearing elsewhere in this file -- it was simply dropped here.

members.why_it_matters: Changing your password after suspecting a session/cookie compromise is a standard remediation step users and support flows rely on. With this change, that remediation silently does nothing: a stolen or leaked session cookie keeps working indefinitely after the password change, undermining the primary purpose of the password-change feature's session-eviction behavior that was deliberately added (and tested) to close this exact gap.
members.fix_hint: Restore session_secret rotation: generate a new session secret, include it in the model_copy update alongside password_hash, persist it, and re-issue the acting user's cookie signed with the new secret (mirroring reset_confirm_post's D-12 pattern) before returning the response.
members.intent_doc_match: Contradicts .planning/milestones/v2.6-phases/58-auth-test-suite/58-SECURITY.md T-58-07/AR-58-02: AR-58-02 ('Password change does not rotate session_secret') was explicitly REVOKED 2026-05-31 after session_secret rotation was added to change_password specifically to close this gap, covered by tests test_password_change_invalidates_old_sessions, test_change_password_rotates_session_secret_and_persists, test_change_password_evicts_other_device_session. This diff reverts that fix.

members.title: Removing the rotation and re-issue breaks five existing auth tests that assert eviction behavior
members.problem: These tests assert behavior this diff removes. In tests/test_auth_routes.py: test_change_password_rotates_session_secret_and_persists (line 604) asserts the persisted secret changed. test_change_password_reissues_acting_user_cookie (line 641) asserts a Set-Cookie on the response. test_change_password_evicts_other_device_session (line 677) asserts the old cookie stops validating. In tests/test_auth_integration.py: test_password_change_invalidates_old_sessions (line 182) asserts the old cookie is rejected. Its docstring says this was a deliberate reversal made on 2026-05-31. The tests were not updated, so the suite fails. Updating them to pass would encode the security regression.
